fixed.what: Master tags removed from Donnas and Carema's shared stone-pillared pergolas: the Codex's Village bank asks Carema's stone-pillared Nebbiolo at the Valle d'Aosta border (c-itbaia89) and ties Donnas to Carema (c-boinaakr), and Piedmont's own Carema place is untagged, so the card and the question are Village reading.

The exam line that put Donnas and Carema at Grand Cru now names the article's master places, Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino and Colline di Levanto; the Carema link joins the untagged line on the valley's grapes.
The untagged card taught the count of seven sub-zones that questions[5] and cards[8] tag advanced and exam[7] puts at Premier Cru; it now says the DOC is labelled with a grape or a named sub-zone.
Over the mountains to the north set the Valle d'Aosta directly behind Liguria's ridges; Piedmont lies between the two, so it now reads beyond Piedmont to the north.
Respelt DOH-rah BAHL-teh-ah: the Italian name is stressed on the first syllable of Baltea.
The Rossese di Dolceacqua disciplinare (DPR 28 January 1972) added as a primary source: the 1972 date of Liguria's first DOC rested on a press piece and reference summaries.

The card of the Superiore's ageing figures (three years, twelve months in wood and twelve in bottle, 13.5 per cent) tagged advanced: the article's own exam[7] and questions[5] put those figures at Premier Cru, and the Village bank asks only the word Superiore (c-ca7ue8nd).

The Riserva's five years was prescribed at Village in an untagged card and exam line while its sibling figures sat at Premier Cru; the card now says a longer aged Riserva, exam[5] reads Superiore and Riserva as the Court's label terms do, and exam[7] names the Superiore's and the Riserva's ageing years as Premier Cru.
Etna and Vesuvius were called the active volcanoes of southern Italian wine, which leaves out the Campi Flegrei, Stromboli and Vulcano; now active volcanoes with vineyards on their slopes.

confirmed: Cirò Classico DOCG (2025, EU publication C/2025/1933 and the implementing regulation of July 2025 by the reports): dry red only, at least 90 per cent Gaglioppo with Magliocco or Greco Nero, from Cirò and Cirò Marina, at least 36 months of ageing with at least six in wood; Calabria's first DOCG (Gambero Rosso, Decanter, Wine Scholar Guild, Italian Wine Central).

Aglianico del Vulture Superiore: DOCG by the decree of 2 August 2010 from the DOC of 1971; three years from 1 November with at least twelve months in wood and twelve in bottle, Riserva from the fifth year, 13.5 per cent minimum alcohol (the disciplinare and Italian Wine Central).

Cirò DOC by DPR of 2 April 1969; whites at least 80 per cent Greco Bianco and reds and rosés at least 80 per cent Gaglioppo in the current text (higher shares in older sources describe the earlier rule).
Rossese di Dolceacqua by DPR of 28 January 1972, Liguria's first DOC; Pornassio or Ormeasco di Pornassio a DOC of its own from 2003, split from Riviera Ligure di Ponente, with a Sciac-trà type.

Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle: Prié Blanc only, ungrafted, on low pergolas that hold the soil's warmth at night, up to about 1,200 metres (some sources say 1,250 or 1,300; the article's about 900 to 1,200 stands).

Every question holds one fact, an unambiguous key and four options of one kind, with no answer in the stem and no key the longest option (Liguria's Dolcetto ties Nebbiolo at eight letters); every card's back answers its front.

The Court's central-southern-italy rows are covered for both regions: Basilicata and Calabria placed between their seas, the Mediterranean south and the cooler Vulture, the Apennines, the Ligurian and Tyrrhenian seas, Aglianico, IGP, DOC and DOCG, Superiore and Riserva, producers and a decanting line for young Aglianico del Vulture; the tuscany row's Ligurian Sea sits in Liguria's water. No CMS subject writes a row for Liguria's wines or the Valle d'Aosta.
open: The Valle d'Aosta as Italy's smallest wine region is kept as a measured superlative: it is smallest by area and by output, and the Codex's Régionale bank asks it (i-ibxlio6l).
Cirò Classico's 13 per cent minimum alcohol and 80 quintals a hectare (one report each) are not added; the Valle d'Aosta DOC stays undated, as the author left it.
One search summary called Ormeasco's Sciac-trà a red; the reference works give it as a rosato, and the article's rosé stands.
Fumin (few-MAN) and Donnas (doh-NAH) keep their French respellings; Italian speakers also stress them on the first syllable, and no audio source was sought.

The aliases barile, monte vulture and rionero in vulture still point to campania in italy.3.json; the integrator may move them to calabria-basilicata, as the author notes.
